Jock
JOK
noun (Gen X slang)
Short for jockstrap, the athletic supporter; by the 1950s–60s American college slang used jock for the athlete himself. In Gen X high schools of the late 1970s and 1980s it named a social tribe — the letter-jacket athletes at the top of the cafeteria — set against nerds, burnouts, and preps; The Breakfast Club (1985) put "an athlete" among its five types. Compounds: dumb jock, jock culture.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A jock is the athlete as a social type: the letter jacket, the gym-built shoulders, the guy who is cheered on Friday night and runs the hallway on Monday. Gen X high schools were organized around jocks, and the word could be admiring or bitter depending on who said it — with dumb jock always ready for the boy who was all muscle and no mind. The Christian observation is that Scripture honors athletic discipline and refuses athletic idolatry. Paul loved sports metaphors: "So run, that ye may obtain" (1Co 9:24), and "every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible" (1Co 9:25). Training, self-denial, playing by the rules — "he is not crowned, except he strive lawfully" (2Ti 2:5) — are real virtues. But the apostle also puts the body in its place: "bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things" (1Ti 4:8). And God is not impressed by the stat sheet: "He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man" (Psa 147:10). The tragedy of the high-school jock is the man whose life peaked at seventeen because his strength was his identity. A father can coach his athletic son hard and cheer him loud, and still teach him the better race — to "run with patience the race that is set before us," "looking unto Jesus" (Heb 12:1-2) — and to use his strength to protect the weaker boy, not to rule over him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Short for jockstrap; 1950s–60s college slang for an athlete and the Gen X high-school tribe of letter-jacket athletes; Scripture honors the disciplined runner (1Co 9:25) but says bodily exercise profiteth little beside godliness (1Ti 4:8).

JOCK, n. (Gen X slang, 1950s–60s college origin, high-school tribe of the late 1970s–1980s, United States) An athlete, especially one whose identity and status rest on sports. "The jocks always sit by the window."

Short for jockstrap, the athletic supporter. Compounds: dumb jock, jock culture; the radio jock (from disc jockey) is a separate word.

Gen X cafeteria tribes: jocks, nerds, preps, burnouts; The Breakfast Club (1985) includes "an athlete."

No entry in Webster 1828; the athletic sense is 20th-century American college slang.

Decode for parents: train and cheer your athlete, but do not let a jersey become his identity — strength is for serving the weak.

Key Scripture

1Co 9:24 — "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain."

1Co 9:25 — "And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible."

2Ti 2:5 — "And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully."

1Ti 4:8 — "For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come."

Psa 147:10 — "He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man."

Modern Corruption

Jock makes athletic strength a social rank and an identity; Scripture honors the disciplined runner but puts bodily exercise beneath godliness.

expand to see more

Strength as status. In the Gen X cafeteria the jocks were royalty, and royalty is a temptation. The strong boy learns that muscle buys deference, and some never learn anything else. Scripture’s rule for strength runs the other way: "We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak" (Rom 15:1). A jock who protects the dweeb has understood what strength is for; the one who stuffs him in a locker has only borrowed it.

The better crown. Paul honors the athlete’s discipline (1Co 9:25) and the rules of the game (2Ti 2:5), then lifts the eyes to an incorruptible crown. The danger is the man who peaked at seventeen and has been reliving Friday nights ever since, because his worth was in his legs, and God "taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man" (Psa 147:10). Bodily exercise profits a little (1Ti 4:8); godliness profits for ever.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Jockstrap → 1950s–60s college jock, an athlete → Gen X high-school tribe → dumb jock; Scripture: an incorruptible crown (1Co 9:25); godliness profitable unto all things (1Ti 4:8).
